title: A New Heaven and a New Earth
lead: History does not end in suffering, death, or decay. God makes all things new.
questions: Whom will you tell this week, as simply as you can, the one sentence that has carried us through these forty days: there is hope?
What are you still trying to buy from God or earn from Him, even though the Bible’s final offer is free?
Which message from these forty days is especially important to you? In what situation in your life should it start to work?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: The story of the Bible begins in a garden and ends in the city of God, where the garden has not vanished but has been regained and transformed. We began by listening to the promise of an offspring who would crush the serpent’s head. Today we open the last pages of the Bible and discover that the last chapters of Revelation answer the first chapters of Genesis point by point. “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth.” The Greek kainos means new in quality, not simply a different one. God does not throw His creation away like a failed project – He renews it. The Creator Himself puts His signature to this promise: “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.”

In the Greek text the words “and the sea was no more” say precisely: that sea. John writes as an old man exiled on Patmos, cut off by water from everyone he loved. In the new world there will be nothing left that separates and threatens. The heart of this vision beats in one sentence: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.” Notice the direction: people are not evacuated upward; the city comes “down out of heaven.” The Bible’s finale is God moving in with us. And His first act after the move: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” Personally, like a mother with her child. The city has a shape that was an easily read code for anyone who knew the Old Testament. Its equal length, width, and height point very clearly to the Most Holy Place, which the high priest entered once a year. In this apocalyptic description the Most Holy Place is stretched out over an entire city. There is no temple there, because all of it is temple.

The river and the tree of life from Eden return too, and “the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” In a world without disease, the last wound to be healed is the division between people. The crowning point of this description is the greatest promise of all: “They will see His face.” That honor was refused to Moses, but the redeemed will receive it. “No longer will there be any curse.” This is not a reward for merit, but the return of what was stolen.

These forty days were meant to teach us one sentence in forty scenes. There is hope. A hope like this cannot be hidden under a basket. All around us are people in their own storms and beside their own empty nets. They don’t want a lecture. They need someone who will sit down by their well and say: there is hope, and I know its name. Jesus!

Forty days ago we began with Eden. We watched trust in God crack, a man hide in the bushes, and the garden gate close behind the first human beings. We also heard the promise that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head. Today, on the last day of our series, we open the final pages of the Bible and discover something planned from the very start – the return to the garden. The last two chapters of Revelation mirror the first three chapters of Genesis, closing a bracket around the whole history of the world. This is no accidental symmetry. It is the story carried through to its end.

sections.heading: I Make All Things New
paragraphs: John writes: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth.” The word “new” is worth pausing over, because Greek expresses newness in two ways. One means new in the sense of “next, different, starting from scratch.” The other, the word kainos, speaks of what is new in quality. That is the word John uses. The new earth is not a replacement planet. It is this same earth, cleansed and restored to the shape it was meant to have. For anyone who loves this world, the difference is enormous. God does not throw His creation away like a failed project – He renews it. “Behold, I make all things new,” says the One seated on the throne, and it is one of the few sentences in Revelation that God speaks in person. Right after it comes a second, which reads like a signature at the bottom of a document: “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.” The hope with which we close this series is not a mood booster or a course in optimism. It is one more promise, bearing God’s own signature.

sections.heading: The Sea Is No More
paragraphs: In the very first sentence of this vision we notice a strange detail: “and the sea was no more.” Why, of all things, should the sea disappear from a perfect world? The Greek text uses the definite article here, which means that particular sea is no more. John writes these words as an old man exiled on Patmos, a rocky island looking out on the water that separated him from all his loved ones and from the churches. To him the sea was not a holiday landscape but a barrier of water cutting him off from those he longed for. In the Bible, from the very beginning, the sea is a picture of chaos and threat. It is an element that had to be subdued. God did this when He created the world, and again when He calmed the storm during the crossing of the lake. So the sentence “the sea was no more” means: nothing is left that separates and threatens. In the new world there will be no water between you and the people you love.

sections.heading: The Dwelling Place of God Is with Man
paragraphs: Then comes the sentence that is the heart not only of this vision but of the whole Bible: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.” Let’s trace this thought, which runs like a golden thread through all the stories. In the wilderness God had a tent built for Himself so He could live in the middle of the camp. Then, as we read in the story from day twenty-eight of our series, “The Word became flesh” – the Lord pitched His tent in human skin. At the end of the biblical account, God’s presence stops being a tent, a temple, or a visit. It becomes a permanent address. Contrary to popular belief, people are not taken up; the city comes “down out of heaven from God.” The Bible’s finale is not an evacuation of people from the earth but the Almighty moving in with people. The same God who asked in Eden, “Where are you?”, who came down to Bethel on the stairway of Jacob’s dream, who took on flesh in Bethlehem, will take the final step: He will move in with us for good. The first thing He does after the move will not be a lecture or a judgment but the tenderest gesture in all of Scripture: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” Not “tears will disappear.” He will wipe them away, personally, the way a mother does for her child. Only then comes the list of what will be no more: death, mourning, crying, and pain. Everything we have talked about in this series, the whole catalog of human misery, comes to an end here.

sections.heading: A City That Is the Most Holy Place
paragraphs: John describes the New Jerusalem in detail and gives measurements that anyone who knew the Old Testament would have decoded at once: the city’s length, width, and height are equal. It is a cube, and in the Bible the Most Holy Place of the temple has the same proportions: the space behind the curtain that the high priest entered once a year. In this apocalyptic description the Most Holy Place is stretched out over the whole city of God. John points out that he saw no temple in that city. He is not speaking of something missing; rather, he is showing that all of it is temple. The earthly building was only ever a promise of an address. The privilege that for centuries belonged to one high priest for a few minutes a year will be the everyday life of all the redeemed. At the moment of Jesus’ death the temple curtain was torn – here we see where that tearing was leading. God removes the curtains so that in the end nothing at all will separate us from Him.

sections.heading: The River and the Tree
paragraphs: In the Bible’s last chapter, exactly the two things that stood at the center of Eden return: a river and the tree of life. The river flows from the throne, and the tree yields fresh fruit every month. There is, however, one new detail: “the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” In a world without disease or death, leaves cannot be healing bodies. The text speaks explicitly of healing nations, not individuals. The last wound God binds up in the Bible is the division between people: national, tribal, racial, linguistic – all the walls humanity has been building since Babel. Our series began with broken trust between human beings and God. It ends with the healing of what has broken between human beings too. There is one more promise here, the greatest: “They will see His face.” That was refused even to Moses, who asked, “Please show me Your glory,” and was told that no one can see God’s face and live. Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, whose name means “face of God,” waited for decades to see the Savior’s face in the face of an infant. Here the waiting of every generation comes to an end – they will see His face, unveiled, without fear, forever. Added to all this is a short sentence from Revelation: “No longer will there be any curse.” The curse of Genesis 3, the thorns, the sweat, the pain, and death, is revoked. This is not a reward for our merits, but the return of the stolen Kingdom.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: So end the forty days of our series, and it is worth asking ourselves why we have traveled this road. Not so we would know more about Noah, Ruth, or Peter. The aim was to learn one sentence in forty scenes: there is hope. When everything has fallen apart and you are at the end of your strength. When you feel like a stranger, a failure, overlooked, stuck. When the boat is sinking, the bread has run out, and the tomb is closing. When the end looks final. In every one of these situations we met the same God. One who comes out to meet people, comes down to where they are, asks, listens, feeds, weeps, calls people by name, and writes the next chapter after our words “The End.” Today’s text speaks of where our journey with Him ends – a home where He will live with us for good. Christian hope is not a fortune-teller’s promise that everything will turn out fine. It is the written promise of the Alpha and the Omega. He is the One who says: “To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life.” Freely. The Bible’s final offer costs nothing, like everything God promises us. For us as a community, this series carries one very important lesson. A hope like this cannot be kept under a basket. All around us live people who are today exactly where the characters in these stories were. In their own storms, beside their own empty nets, on the road to their own Emmaus. They don’t want a lecture from us. They need someone who will sit down by their well and say: there is hope. I know its name. Jesus!
